blocks.html: A penalty, assuredly, as has been shown above, worthy of so detestable a lecher and heinous traitor a3. For hanging on the gibbet is, of all the punishments the ancients were able to devise, the most foul, ignominious, base and infamous: wherefore the Poets have called such a death base, filthy, ugly, unsightly and wretched. As Virgil, speaking of Amata, mother of Lavinia, who, indignant against her daughter, whom Aeneas had married (although she and King Latinus her father had pledged her to Turnus), hanged and strangled herself, saying b2,

notes.citation: Accursius (Glossa ordinaria) on Digest 49.16.3 (De re militari, l. 3, Modestinus); Baldus on the fragment Cum quidam in the title De iureiurando (Digest 12.2, or Code 4.1 De rebus creditis et iureiurando) — fragment not identified
notes.original: Accurſe en la l. iij. D. de re mili. Baldé en la l. cũ qui dã. de iureiur.
notes.gloss: For the point "shown above", that hanging is the most infamous of deaths; the Gloss on D. 49.16.3, which lists the soldier's penalties, is where the glossators rank the furca.
Et nodum informis leti trabe nectit ab alta: Amata's suicide; the print's nondum is a slip for nodum.

blocks.html: And she knots from a high beam the noose of an unsightly death (Et nodum informis leti trabe nectit ab alta).

Achaeus also, king of Lydia, because he overburdened his people with great tributes and insupportable charges, was, in a popular sedition, to the perpetual ignominy of himself, of his posterity and of such tyrants, hanged with his feet uppermost and his head hanging over the river Pactolus, whose sand is of gold. Which Ovid eloquently expresses when he says e:

notes.citation: Ovid, Ibis, lines 299–300 (the numbering varies by edition)
notes.gloss: Morte vel intereas capti suspensus Achaei, / qui miser aurifera teste pependit aqua: the print's Onide is Ouide, and its reſte is the editions' teste.

blocks.html: Or may you perish by the death of captive Achaeus, hanged, who, wretched, hung by a rope over the gold-bearing water (Morte vel intereas, capti suspensus Achaei, Qui miser aurifera reste pependit aqua).

And in the books of the Roman Pontiffs it was ordained, among other things, that the bodies of the hanged, as abominable, should have no burial, but should be, as in disdain, thrown upon the ground, to be eaten and devoured by birds, dogs and other famished beasts.
